grades.reason: Describes the xv6 process address space and page permissions, but not how the kernel safely copies a system-call argument string from user memory.

grades.quote:
fetchstr calls copyinstr to do the hard work.

copyinstr (1833) copies up to max bytes to dst from virtual address srcva in the user page table pagetable. Since pagetable is _not_ the current page table, copyinstr uses walkaddr (which calls walk) to look up srcva in pagetable, yielding physical address pa0.
grades.reason: Directly answers the query. fetchstr calls copyinstr, which uses walkaddr to look up the user virtual address in the user page table and checks that it lies in the process's user address space. The kernel then copies the bytes from the resulting physical address.

grades.quote: Xv6 avoids them in order to reduce the chances of security bugs in the kernel due to inadvertent use of user pointers
grades.reason: Gives background on why xv6 does not let kernel code dereference user pointers directly. It does not describe the safe string-copy mechanism itself.
Covers POSIX mmap file I/O in a general OS textbook. It has nothing to do with xv6 copying system-call argument strings from user memory.
